body:
This item is kinda vague to test and we need to revise this. For example, literally every NodeJS application would fail, because NPM packages are not sandboxed by design.

| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **14.2.6** | Verify that the attack surface is reduced by sandboxing or encapsulating third party libraries to expose only the required behaviour into the application. ([C2](https://owasp.org/www-project-proactive-controls/#div-numbering)) | | ✓ | ✓ | 265 |

I couldn't find more information about this. It seems to be introduced by @tghosth in [Add encaspulation req from proactive controls · OWASP/ASVS@c5934b5](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/commit/c5934b53a203ce6c5a3344de9913bf698df28fde). But the [OWASP proactive controls](https://github.com/OWASP/www-project-proactive-controls/blob/master/v3/en/c2-leverage-security-frameworks-libraries.md) are not more specific.

It would be nice if leftpad couldn't do HTTP requests, but currently there is no framework in any language that I know of that could accomplish this. I say we remove this requirement.
Instead of removing, we can think about it as level 3 requirement.

@elarlang Could you explain how this control could be implemented? We have not seen support for sandboxing in any language other than Java which they are considering to [deprecate](https://inside.java/2021/04/23/security-and-sandboxing-post-securitymanager/) that.

Ok, I understand the concept here but it is a little tricky to implement. As a first suggestion, I would propose the following alterations which include changing this to a L3 requirement and changing the CWE to [1061](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1061.html) which is not an exact match but is closer.

| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **14.2.6** | [MODIFIED, SPLIT TO 14.2.8]  Verify that risky third party libraries or those with a history of vulnerabilities are encapsulated such that only required behaviour is available to the application, to reduce attack surface. ([C2](https://owasp.org/www-project-proactive-controls/#div-numbering)) | | | ✓ | 1061 |
| **14.2.8** | [ADDED, SPLIT FROM 14.2.6] Verify that risky third party libraries or those with a history of vulnerabilities are sandboxed away from the most sensitive system modules/services so that even if a vulnerability in the library was successfully exploited, the  sensitive system modules/services would not be compromised. ([C2](https://owasp.org/www-project-proactive-controls/#div-numbering)) | | | ✓ | 1061 |

I would also suggest adding the following reference to the bottom as it is a good explanation for 14.2.6:
https://www.slideshare.net/KatyAnton1/tips-to-reduce-the-attack-surface-when-using-thirdparty-libraries

Would be great to get some thoughts from @katyanton who wrote that explanation :)
See also https://rlbox.dev/

Ok @Sjord @ImanSharaf @elarlang what do you think about the proposal in my comment above: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1425#issuecomment-1402168268 

?

I'm not an expert on sandboxing in code level, so I'm not too helpful here.

From proposed requirements - it is not clear, what is and how to define "risky third party library" or what exactly makes library history to match this criteria. Also, I think we have requirements which ask to not use libraries with known vulnerabilities like:
* V14.2.1 Verify that all components are up to date, preferably using a dependency checker during build or compile time.
* V14.2.4 Verify that third party components come from pre-defined, trusted and continually maintained repositories.


What I can think of, is that those "riksy libraries" are used as separate service and this is the way those are "sandboxed" from rest of the application code.

I contend that sandboxing third-party libraries is a feature supported by only a limited number of languages or frameworks. Additionally, the proposed requirements do not provide a clear definition or criteria for determining a 'risky third-party library'.

This is a requirement that is just a feature of object-oriented languages.... heck you can write a "Wrapper class" in any language. Frankly, this is a good requirement and I've been doing it in dev for years and the benefits are significant.

Thank you for sharing your valuable insights @jmanico . I recognize and value the benefits of writing wrapper classes, especially in the context of object-oriented languages. The practice is indeed powerful and beneficial in many scenarios.

However, my concern is more specific to certain technologies and frameworks, such as NodeJS and NextJS. When third-party libraries are imported into these types of applications, the libraries often gain access to the application's context. A wrapper class doesn't inherently prevent the third-party code from accessing or spying on that context. The nature of these frameworks makes it challenging to achieve true encapsulation or sandboxing as envisioned by the ASVS requirement.

For instance, in a NodeJS environment, even if we wrap a third-party library within our custom class, the third-party code can potentially access variables, other modules, and more from our application's context. The challenge is beyond just a wrapper class; it's about the depth of isolation we can achieve, which varies depending on the framework and language.

I believe it's essential to consider these nuances when defining security standards to ensure that they are practically applicable across various tech stacks.

Well, you can explain here for me or for whoever asks. The requirement text should be as "one interpretation only" as it is possible. At the moment everyone can define their own "risky".

We have requirements like 14.2.1 and 14.2.4 (see https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1425#issuecomment-1717388166), and we have added 14.2.7:
_V14.2.7 [ADDED] Verify that third party components are sourced separately from internally owned and developed applications._

Proposed requirements are level 3 - my question is, are there any possible way to use "risky" libraries for level 3 application? I guess not really. Maybe those requirements should be applied for every 3rd party library?

> Well, you can explain here for me or for whoever asks. The requirement text should be as "one interpretation only" as it is possible. At the moment everyone can define their own "risky".

We can think about how we make the definition of risky clearer although it might create a long requirement. On the other hand, maybe they should have that documented which would fall into V1....

> Proposed requirements are level 3 - my question is, are there any possible way to use "risky" libraries for level 3 application? I guess not really. Maybe those requirements should be applied for every 3rd party library?

I take your point but I think the idea here is realistically there are always likely to be risky libraries in 3rd party apps so here we are providing the requirements (which are quite hard to implement) in order to do this.
I shared my concerns based on text, those does not make too much sense for me. Till those are level 3 requirements,I'm ok with those.

> I shared my concerns based on text, those does not make too much sense for me. Till those are level 3 requirements,I'm ok with those.

So @elarlang you think we should have a V1 requirement where the developers define which libraries they have categorised as risky or do you think we can just leave them as level 3 requirements in V14?
My point is more, that I don't think it's too reasonable and if it is level 3 requirement, it is so niche that I don't care too much.
